item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
No subjects taken through SCP-864 have been recovered.

So how is this thing pulling people through an 8 inch opening? Or does it pull them so hard it crushes their bodies to be able to fit that size?

The idea is cool, but it could use a further rewrite for overall tone, I feel…it's not bad, but for some reason it doesn't catch1 me.

Why would you need to keep the room completely dry if the basin needs at least 200ml water in it to work? Are we implying "water" could be in any form (solid, liquid or gaseous) for activating it, or do we just fear that enough humidity might condense to make up 200ml of liquid water? Unless the Foundation is set in a rainforest (and even then), I don't think the latter is very likely; also, if the idea of any amount of water in it seems, to Researchers, as "ZOMG-K END OF REALITY SCE-NO-RIO" as would be playing dodge447-1 against a horde of zombies, you could just have a D-class go in there, like, once every two months and dry the moisture with a towel, and you'd still be good to go. Assuming, of course, that the washbasin doesn't have a second anomalous property of actively looking for water with any means available, or maybe supercondensation, but if that's the case you'd need to actually say it in the entry and elaborate on it (does it only condensate/look for water? Is there a specific, known reason why it doesn't condensate, say, oxygen or nitrogen, if it doesn't?).

Does it only work with tap water? I can't believe the Researchers wouldn't try filling it with, say, seawater, or maybe lemonade. Do the extremities change in relation to the amount of water, source of the water, purity of the water, presence and/or amount of soap in the water? What happens if you put it under an open tap and let it overflow, or if you dunk it into a pool? Does anything at all happen if you put a water-free liquid in it, like pure ethanol or lava? Experiments

Neutral vote. As said, the idea is cool and Sorts of creepy, but it could use further improvement.

Footnotes
1. I only realized what I said after saying it. #sorrynotsorry

item.content:encoded:
Um, no.

Safe = If you put it in a box and forget about it, it doesn't do anything. Therefore, you can leave it alone.

Euclid = If you put it in a box and forget about it, it does things. Therefore, it requires maintenance.

Keter = If you put it in a box and forget about it, all hell breaks loose. Therefore, it requires continual effort to keep all hell from breaking loose.

We have plenty of easily-contained Euclids.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This needs to be classified as safe.

Safe=fully contained (contained, no influences to use it, easy to turn off, etc)
Euclid=hard/impossible to contain (destroys it's containment, too big to contain, etc)
Keter=risk of breach (breaking out of containment, releasing other SCP, leaking secure/classified things related to the foundation, exponential effect, risk of end of the world disaster, etc)

No matter how dangerous it is, if you can contain it, it is safe. No matter how safe something is, if you can't contain it, it's euclid. If it can cause a disaster by escaping, directly or indirectly, it is keter.
